claim: The rodent visual system has attracted great interest in recent years due to its experimental tractability.
source: The rodent visual system has attracted great interest in recent years due to its experimental tractability, but the fundamental mechanisms used by the mouse to represent the visual world remain unclear.
evidence: This is a general statement about the field that is widely acknowledged in neuroscience research.

claim: The fundamental mechanisms used by the mouse to represent the visual world remain unclear.
source: The rodent visual system has attracted great interest in recent years due to its experimental tractability, but the fundamental mechanisms used by the mouse to represent the visual world remain unclear.
evidence: This is stated as a motivation for the study and represents the state of knowledge prior to this work.

claim: In the primate, a key step in visual representation is 'figure-ground segmentation', the delineation of figures as distinct from backgrounds.
source: In the primate, researchers have argued from both behavioral and neural evidence that a key step in visual representation is 'figure-ground segmentation', the delineation of figures as distinct from backgrounds.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to existing research literature on primate vision.

claim: Mice were severely limited in their ability to segment figure from ground using the opponent motion cue.
source: Unlike primates, mice were severely limited in their ability to segment figure from ground using the opponent motion cue, with segmentation behavior strongly dependent on the specific carrier pattern.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by behavioral experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Mouse segmentation behavior was strongly dependent on the specific carrier pattern.
source: Unlike primates, mice were severely limited in their ability to segment figure from ground using the opponent motion cue, with segmentation behavior strongly dependent on the specific carrier pattern.
evidence: This finding is demonstrated by the behavioral data in Figure 2, showing different performance across Cross, Iso, and Nat conditions.

claim: When mice were forced to localize naturalistic patterns defined by opponent motion, they adopted a strategy of brute force memorization of texture patterns.
source: Remarkably, when mice were forced to localize naturalistic patterns defined by opponent motion, they adopted a strategy of brute force memorization of texture patterns.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral experiments showing that mice could perform the task with trained textures but failed to generalize to new textures (Figure 2e-g).

claim: Primates, including humans, macaques, and mouse lemurs, could readily segment figures independent of carrier pattern using the opponent motion cue.
source: In contrast, primates, including humans, macaques, and mouse lemurs, could readily segment figures independent of carrier pattern using the opponent motion cue.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from macaques and mouse lemurs shown in Figure 2i3-i4.

claim: Neural responses in mouse visual areas V1, RL, and LM did not support texture-invariant segmentation of figures using opponent motion.
source: Consistent with mouse behavior, neural responses to the same stimuli recorded in mouse visual areas V1, RL, and LM also did not support texture-invariant segmentation of figures using opponent motion.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology and imaging data shown in Figures 3-5.

claim: The texture dependence of both the mouse's behavior and neural responses could be explained by a feedforward neural network lacking explicit segmentation capabilities.
source: Modeling revealed that the texture dependence of both the mouse's behavior and neural responses could be explained by a feedforward neural network lacking explicit segmentation capabilities.
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 7.

claim: Mice use visual cues for important behaviors such as hunting, evasion, and navigation.
source: Mice, in contrast, rely far less on their visual system, though they do use visual cues for important behaviors such as hunting, evasion, and navigation (Evans et al., 2018; Fiser et al., 2016; Harvey et al., 2012; Hoy et al., 2016; Leinweber et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Visual responses in mouse visual cortex share low-level organizing principles with those of primate visual cortex, including temporal/spatial frequency tuning.
source: While work has shown that visual responses in mouse visual cortex share low-level organizing principles with those of primate visual cortex, including temporal/spatial frequency tuning (Marshel et al., 2011), orientation selectivity (Niell and Stryker, 2008), and contextual surround effects (Self et al., 2014; Keller et al., 2020a), it remains unclear to what extent the two species share more abstract representations of visual objects and scenes.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Marshel et al., 2011.

claim: Visual responses in mouse visual cortex share orientation selectivity with primate visual cortex.
source: While work has shown that visual responses in mouse visual cortex share low-level organizing principles with those of primate visual cortex, including temporal/spatial frequency tuning (Marshel et al., 2011), orientation selectivity (Niell and Stryker, 2008), and contextual surround effects (Self et al., 2014; Keller et al., 2020a), it remains unclear to what extent the two species share more abstract representations of visual objects and scenes.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Niell and Stryker, 2008.

claim: Visual responses in mouse visual cortex share contextual surround effects with primate visual cortex.
source: While work has shown that visual responses in mouse visual cortex share low-level organizing principles with those of primate visual cortex, including temporal/spatial frequency tuning (Marshel et al., 2011), orientation selectivity (Niell and Stryker, 2008), and contextual surround effects (Self et al., 2014; Keller et al., 2020a), it remains unclear to what extent the two species share more abstract representations of visual objects and scenes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Self et al., 2014 and Keller et al., 2020a.

claim: It remains unclear to what extent mice and primates share more abstract representations of visual objects and scenes.
source: While work has shown that visual responses in mouse visual cortex share low-level organizing principles with those of primate visual cortex, including temporal/spatial frequency tuning (Marshel et al., 2011), orientation selectivity (Niell and Stryker, 2008), and contextual surround effects (Self et al., 2014; Keller et al., 2020a), it remains unclear to what extent the two species share more abstract representations of visual objects and scenes.
evidence: This represents the knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: In primates, segmentation is a key step in visual processing following early feature extraction.
source: In primates, segmentation is a key step in visual processing following early feature extraction (Frost and Nakayama, 1983; He and Nakayama, 1992; Lamme, 1995; Williford and von der Heydt, 2013; Zhou et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research on primate vision.

claim: The primate visual system performs segmentation by generating a surface representation, an assignment of each retinal pixel to a distinct contiguous surface situated in 3D space.
source: A large body of psychophysics suggests that the primate visual system performs segmentation by generating a surface representation, an assignment of each retinal pixel to a distinct contiguous surface situated in 3D space (He and Nakayama, 1992; Tsao and Tsao, 2022; Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1a.

claim: Accretion-deletion is the appearance or disappearance of pixels forming the background surface due to motion or binocular disparity of the foreground surface.
source: Aiding this goal, there is one cue that is unambiguous: accretion–deletion, the appearance or disappearance of pixels forming the background surface due to motion (or binocular disparity) of the foreground surface (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a definition supported by reference to Figure 1b.

claim: Gibson identified accretion-deletion as the single most important cue to surface organization because it is unambiguous, invariant to texture, and locally available.
source: Gibson identified accretion–deletion as the single most important cue to surface organization because it is unambiguous, invariant to texture, and locally available (Gibson, 1979).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gibson, 1979.

claim: Psychophysical experiments in humans demonstrate that accretion-deletion alone is able to evoke a vivid percept of an object border.
source: Psychophysical experiments in humans demonstrate that accretion–deletion alone is able to evoke a vivid percept of an object border (Nakayama and Shimojo, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nakayama and Shimojo, 1990.

claim: Neurons in primate V1, V2, and V4 modulate their firing according to whether a stimulus is part of the foreground or background.
source: Neurons in primate V1, V2, and V4 modulate their firing according to whether a stimulus is part of the foreground or background (Lamme, 1995; Poort et al., 2012; Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research and illustrated in Figure 1c.

claim: Border-ownership cells have been found in macaque areas V2 and V4 that explicitly signal object borders.
source: Complementing figure-ground signaling, a population of neurons have been found in macaque areas V2 and V4 that explicitly signal object borders. These 'border-ownership' cells respond selectively to figure edges, including those defined purely by accretion–deletion, and are moreover modulated by the side of the figure relative to the edge (Zhou et al., 2000; Qiu and von der Heydt, 2005; Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhou et al., 2000 and Qiu and von der Heydt, 2005, and illustrated in Figure 1c.

claim: Border-ownership cells respond selectively to figure edges, including those defined purely by accretion-deletion.
source: These 'border-ownership' cells respond selectively to figure edges, including those defined purely by accretion–deletion, and are moreover modulated by the side of the figure relative to the edge (Zhou et al., 2000; Qiu and von der Heydt, 2005; Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1c.

claim: Mice are capable of texture-based segmentation, in which figure and background are defined by grating patterns with different orientation and/or phase.
source: Behaviorally, mice are capable of texture-based segmentation, in which figure and background are defined by grating patterns with different orientation and/or phase (Kirchberger et al., 2020; Schnabel et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Cells in mouse V1 show iso-orientation surround suppression.
source: Consistent with this behavioral capability, cells in mouse V1 show iso-orientation surround suppression (Self et al., 2014; Keller et al., 2020a) and have been reported to be modulated by figure versus ground (Schnabel et al., 2018a; Kirchberger et al., 2020; Keller et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Self et al., 2014 and Keller et al., 2020a.

claim: Cells in mouse V1 have been reported to be modulated by figure versus ground.
source: Consistent with this behavioral capability, cells in mouse V1 show iso-orientation surround suppression (Self et al., 2014; Keller et al., 2020a) and have been reported to be modulated by figure versus ground (Schnabel et al., 2018a; Kirchberger et al., 2020; Keller et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schnabel et al., 2018a, Kirchberger et al., 2020, and Keller et al., 2020b.

claim: Previous studies of mouse figure-ground segmentation have used texture-based cues, which are fundamentally ambiguous for solving segmentation.
source: However, all these studies have used texture-based cues, which are fundamentally ambiguous for solving segmentation (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a critical assessment of previous work, supported by reference to Figure 1b showing the ambiguity of texture cues.

claim: Behavioral evidence demonstrates that primates possess a mechanism for explicit, cue-invariant segmentation exploiting accretion-deletion.
source: In contrast, behavioral evidence unequivocally demonstrates that primates possess a mechanism for explicit, cue-invariant segmentation exploiting accretion–deletion (Nakayama and Shimojo, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nakayama and Shimojo, 1990.

claim: Mice quickly learned the Cross task, reaching 88% performance after 7 days.
source: Mice quickly learned the Cross task, reaching 88% performance after 7 days.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Mice were slightly slower to learn the Iso task, reaching 77% performance after 9 days.
source: They were slightly slower to learn the Iso task, reaching 77% performance after 9 days.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Mice struggled to effectively learn the Nat task, reaching only around 71% performance after 13 days.
source: However, they struggled to effectively learn the Nat task, reaching only around 71% performance after 13 days.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Macaque monkeys performed at >90% for all three conditions (Cross, Iso, Nat) within the first session.
source: The monkeys performed at >90% for all three conditions within the first session (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Three out of four mice successfully learned to detect the square in the full Nat condition after gradual shaping over 26 training sessions.
source: By the end of 26 training sessions, three out of four mice successfully learned to detect the square in the full Nat condition (Figure 2e, '100%').
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Mice performed near chance (60% mean performance) on seven new textures in the Nat condition.
source: To our surprise, the mice performed near chance on these new textures (Figure 2f, mean performance across three mice that had learned the task: 60%; test for significant difference between performance on new textures and performance on last day of noise shaping: p < 0.01 for each mouse, Chi-square test).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2f.

claim: Mice displayed no change in performance upon removal of motion in the Nat stimulus.
source: Astonishingly, this turned out to be the case: mice displayed no change in performance upon removal of motion in the stimulus, which completely removed any way of inferring a figure (Figure 2g, mean performance across three mice that had learned the task: 87%; test for significant difference between performance on static textures and performance on last day of noise shaping: p > 0.01 for each mouse, Chi-square test).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2g.

claim: Mice showed no drop in behavioral performance for any of the three conditions (Cross, Iso, Nat) when motion was removed.
source: As before, these mice showed no drop in behavioral performance for any of the three conditions (Figure 2h, Cross: p = 0.67, Iso: p = 0.02 (increasing), Nat: p = 0.26), confirming that the animals were not using the motion cue for figure detection.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2h.

claim: Monkeys showed a dramatic drop in performance when motion cues were removed from the Nat stimulus.
source: For the Nat condition, however, monkeys showed a dramatic drop in performance when motion cues were removed from the stimulus (Figure 2h, Fisher's exact test, p-vals, Monkey 1: Cross: 1.0, Iso: 0.41, Nat: 9.7e−14; Monkey 2: Cross: 0.77, Iso: 0.75, Nat: 2.2e−19).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2h.

claim: Mice were able to generalize well for the Cross condition with a mean performance drop of 2.47%.
source: We found that mice were able to generalize well for the Cross condition (Figure 2i1, left, mean performance drop = 2.47%), and moderately well for the Iso condition (mean performance drop = 6.55%).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2i1.

claim: Mice generalized moderately well for the Iso condition with a mean performance drop of 6.55%.
source: We found that mice were able to generalize well for the Cross condition (Figure 2i1, left, mean performance drop = 2.47%), and moderately well for the Iso condition (mean performance drop = 6.55%).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2i1.

claim: For the Nat condition, mouse performance dropped almost to chance with a mean performance drop of 20.61%.
source: However, for the Nat condition, performance dropped almost to chance (mean performance drop = 20.61%; p = 0.0011, ranksum test), consistent with the result of our previous experiment (Figure 2f).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2i1.

claim: Treeshrews performed similar to mice, displaying generalization for the Cross and Iso conditions but not the Nat condition.
source: The treeshrews performed similar to mice, displaying generalization for the Cross and Iso conditions but not the Nat condition (Figure 2i2).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2i2.

claim: Mouse lemurs were readily able to generalize for all three conditions (Cross, Iso, Nat).
source: In contrast, and similar to macaques, the mouse lemurs were readily able to generalize for all three conditions (Figure 2i3), implying that they, like the macaques (Figure 2i4), were able to perform visual segmentation using the opponent motion cue.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2i3.

claim: Macaques were able to generalize to unseen patterns for all three conditions (Cross, Iso, Nat).
source: The macaques showed a very different behavioral pattern compared to the mice: they were able to generalize to unseen patterns for all three conditions, indicating that they were capable of performing segmentation using the opponent motion cue, and had not simply memorized the texture pattern in the Nat condition like the mice.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2i4.

claim: The peak acuity of macaque fovea is 5 cpd.
source: The peak acuities of the four species studied vary over two orders of magnitude: 5 cpd (macaque fovea, Merigan et al., 1991), 0.5 cpd (mouse lemur, Ho et al., 2021), 0.5 cpd (treeshrew, Petry et al., 1984), and 0.05 cpd (mouse, Prusky et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Merigan et al., 1991.

claim: The peak acuity of mouse lemur is 0.5 cpd.
source: The peak acuities of the four species studied vary over two orders of magnitude: 5 cpd (macaque fovea, Merigan et al., 1991), 0.5 cpd (mouse lemur, Ho et al., 2021), 0.5 cpd (treeshrew, Petry et al., 1984), and 0.05 cpd (mouse, Prusky et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ho et al., 2021.

claim: The peak acuity of treeshrew is 0.5 cpd.
source: The peak acuities of the four species studied vary over two orders of magnitude: 5 cpd (macaque fovea, Merigan et al., 1991), 0.5 cpd (mouse lemur, Ho et al., 2021), 0.5 cpd (treeshrew, Petry et al., 1984), and 0.05 cpd (mouse, Prusky et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Petry et al., 1984.

claim: The peak acuity of mouse is 0.05 cpd.
source: The peak acuities of the four species studied vary over two orders of magnitude: 5 cpd (macaque fovea, Merigan et al., 1991), 0.5 cpd (mouse lemur, Ho et al., 2021), 0.5 cpd (treeshrew, Petry et al., 1984), and 0.05 cpd (mouse, Prusky et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Prusky et al., 2000.

claim: Mouse and treeshrew visual acuity differ by an order of magnitude, yet neither species could perform the Nat task.
source: First, mouse and treeshrew visual acuity differ by an order of magnitude, yet neither species could perform the task.
evidence: This is an inference from the behavioral data and visual acuity measurements, arguing against visual acuity as the limiting factor.

claim: The treeshrew and mouse lemur have identical visual acuity, yet the mouse lemur could perform the task while the treeshrew could not.
source: Second, even more compellingly, the treeshrew and mouse lemur have identical visual acuity, yet the mouse lemur could perform the task while the treeshrew could not.
evidence: This is an inference from the behavioral data and visual acuity measurements, providing strong evidence against visual acuity as the limiting factor.

claim: 23-52% of the stimulus energy in the Nat stimulus had frequency less than 0.064 cpd when the mouse position varied from 23 to 1 cm from the screen.
source: Importantly, 23–52% of the stimulus energy in the Nat stimulus had frequency less than 0.064 cpd, the peak contrast sensitivity of the mouse (Prusky et al., 2000), when the mouse position varied from 23 to 1 cm from the screen.
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of the stimulus properties relative to mouse visual capabilities.

claim: The fact that the mouse could learn to distinguish the Nat patterns after extensive training demonstrates that the mouse could perceive the spatial frequencies present in the Nat stimulus.
source: Fourth, the fact that the mouse could learn to distinguish the Nat patterns after extensive training (Figure 2c) directly demonstrates that the mouse could perceive the spatial frequencies present in the Nat stimulus.
evidence: This is an inference from the behavioral data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Mice learned a modified Nat task in which the background was static much more quickly, indicating that they could see the motion cue.
source: To control for this, we trained the same eight mice as in Figure 2i1 to perform the Nat condition in a modified situation in which the background was static. The animals learned this modified Nat task much more quickly, indicating that they could see the motion cue (Figure 2—figure supplement 2c); their deficit was specific to seeing the figure defined by opponent motion.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2c.

claim: No neuron in V1, LM, or RL showed high correspondence across all six stimulus conditions tested, indicative of a texture-invariant figure response.
source: No neuron in any area showed high correspondence (signified by non-zero mean) across all conditions tested, indicative of a texture-invariant figure response.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of neural data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The mean Pearson correlation between figure maps across all possible pairs from the six conditions was centered around 0 (V1: 0.032, LM: 0.034, RL: 0.015).
source: To quantify this across the population, we computed distributions of the mean Pearson correlation between figure maps across all possible pairs from the six conditions: the values were centered around 0 (V1: 0.032, LM: 0.034, RL: 0.015) (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of neural data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Distributions of FGM indices were approximately centered on zero, with a slight rightward shift for Cross (Cross: 0.07, Iso: −0.014, Nat: −0.03).
source: Distributions of FGM indices were approximately centered on zero, with a slight rightward shift for Cross (Cross: 0.07, Iso: −0.014, Nat: −0.03) (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of neural data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: No neurons showed significant figure modulation across more than three conditions.
source: We found no neurons that showed significant figure modulation across more than three conditions (Figure 5e).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of neural data shown in Figure 5e.

claim: Distributions of BOM indices were approximately centered on zero (Cross: −0.02, Iso: −0.01, Nat: −0.07).
source: Distributions of BOM indices were approximately centered on zero (Cross: −0.02, Iso: −0.01, Nat: −0.07) (Figure 5g).
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of neural data shown in Figure 5g.

claim: No neurons showed significant BOM across more than three conditions.
source: We found no neurons that showed significant BOM across more than three conditions (Figure 5h).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of neural data shown in Figure 5h.

claim: There was clear enhancement in response to the figure/border versus ground for the Cross condition starting at the earliest time point of response.
source: While there was clear enhancement in response to the figure/border versus ground for the Cross condition starting at the earliest time point of response (Figure 5i), differences were much smaller for Iso and Nat conditions (Figure 5j, k).
evidence: This is supported by time course analysis shown in Figure 5i.

claim: Differences in response to figure/border versus ground were much smaller for Iso and Nat conditions compared to Cross.
source: While there was clear enhancement in response to the figure/border versus ground for the Cross condition starting at the earliest time point of response (Figure 5i), differences were much smaller for Iso and Nat conditions (Figure 5j, k).
evidence: This is supported by time course analysis shown in Figures 5j and 5k.

claim: Using electrophysiology data, neural decoding was best for the Cross condition (r2 = 0.89 for 200 cells), followed by Iso (r2 = 0.53 for 200 cells), and then Nat (r2 = 0.09 for 200 cells).
source: Using electrophysiology data, we found that on average neural decoding was best for the Cross condition (r2 = 0.89 for 200 cells), followed by Iso (r2 = 0.53 for 200 cells), and then Nat (r2 = 0.09 for 200 cells).
evidence: This is supported by decoding analysis shown in Figure 6c.

claim: The dependence of position decoding on texture condition (Cross > Iso > Nat) matched the ranking observed in the behavioral performance of animals on the generalization stage of the figure localization task.
source: This dependence of position decoding on texture condition (Cross > Iso > Nat) matched the ranking observed in the behavioral performance of animals on the generalization stage of the figure localization task (Figure 2i1).
evidence: This is an inference connecting neural decoding results to behavioral performance.

claim: For both the Cross and Iso conditions, decoding was best for LM followed by V1 and RL.
source: For both the Cross and Iso conditions, decoding was best for LM followed by V1 and RL (for N = 120 cells: Cross: LM > RL: p < 10−4, LM > V1: p < 10−4, V1 > RL: n.s.; Iso: LM > RL: p < 10−4, LM > V1: p < 10−4, V1 > RL: p < 10−4, rank sum test) (Figure 6e).
evidence: This is supported by decoding analysis and statistical tests shown in Figure 6e.

claim: A feedforward LN model could robustly decode figure position for the Cross condition, though not for the Iso and Nat conditions.
source: Surprisingly, we found that we could robustly decode figure position for the Cross condition, though not for the Iso and Nat conditions (Figure 7b).
evidence: This is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 7b.

claim: Adding an orientation-dependent divisive term to the LN model to mimic iso-orientation surround suppression yielded more robust decoding in the Cross condition, but did not improve decoding in the Iso or Nat conditions.
source: This surround model behaved similar to our feedforward LN model, failing to capture the texture dependence of the neural and behavioral data from the mouse (Figure 7c).
evidence: This is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 7c.

claim: In mid to late layers (3-5) of a deep convolutional network (VGG16), decoding performance was best for Cross, followed by Iso and then Nat, mirroring mouse behavioral performance and neural data.
source: The performance of the DCN matched the mouse's neural and behavioral data well: performance was best for Cross, followed by Iso, and then Nat, with this preference emerging in mid to late layers of the network.
evidence: This is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 7e.

claim: A deep convolutional network replicated the rank ordering of the mouse's behavior and neural decoding performance (Cross > Iso > Nat).
source: Thus a DCN replicated the rank ordering of the mouse's behavior and neural decoding performance (Cross > Iso > Nat).
evidence: This is a summary of the modeling results from Figure 7e.

claim: The mouse visual system may use similar nonlinear interactions as in a feedforward deep network to accomplish object detection.
source: This suggests the possibility that the mouse visual system may use similar nonlinear interactions as in a feedforward deep network to accomplish object detection.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the modeling results.

claim: Mice and primates segment visual input using fundamentally different strategies.
source: We have shown that mice and primates segment visual input using fundamentally different strategies.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion supported by the behavioral and neural data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Unlike primates, mice are unable to detect figures defined purely by opponent motion.
source: Unlike primates, mice are unable to detect figures defined purely by opponent motion, and hence mouse segmentation behavior is strongly dependent on texture cues (Figure 7f).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7f.

claim: The strong texture dependence of mouse object detection behavior was consistent with neural signals recorded in mouse visual areas V1, RL, and LM.
source: The strong texture dependence of mouse object detection behavior was consistent with neural signals recorded in mouse visual areas V1, RL, and LM, and could be explained by a simple feedforward deep network model lacking explicit segmentation capabilities (Figure 7g).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion supported by neural data shown in Figure 7g.

claim: Only the two primate species (macaque and mouse lemur) could perform segmentation using opponent motion, while mice and treeshrews could not.
source: When we tested three additional species, the macaque, mouse lemur, and treeshrew, using the same paradigm, we found that only the two primate species could perform segmentation using opponent motion.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from Figure 2i1-i4.

claim: The mouse lemur could segment purely motion-defined figures well above chance, while the treeshrew could not.
source: It was especially surprising that the mouse lemur, a tiny (~60–80 g) prosimian primate species (Ho et al., 2021), could segment purely motion-defined figures well above chance, while the treeshrew (~120–200 g), an animal with a much more highly developed visual system than the mouse (Wong and Kaas, 2009; Mustafar et al., 2018; Van Hooser et al., 2013), could not.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from Figure 2i2-i3 and citations about visual system development.

claim: The findings reveal a fundamental difference in the computational strategy used by mice/treeshrews versus primates for visual segmentation.
source: Overall, our findings reveal a fundamental difference in the computational strategy used by mice/treeshrews versus primates for visual segmentation and suggest that surface perception from accretion–deletion may be a capability unique to primates.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the behavioral data across species.

claim: Surface perception from accretion-deletion may be a capability unique to primates.
source: Overall, our findings reveal a fundamental difference in the computational strategy used by mice/treeshrews versus primates for visual segmentation and suggest that surface perception from accretion–deletion may be a capability unique to primates.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the comparative behavioral data.

claim: Visual surface representation is a fundamental step in primate visual processing.
source: We believe this is highly significant because visual surface representation is a fundamental step in primate visual processing (Nakayama et al., 1995; Roe et al., 2012; Tsao and Tsao, 2022), and accretion–deletion (Figure 1b, c) has been recognized since the seminal work of J.J. Gibson as the most powerful cue supporting visual surface representation (Gibson, 1979).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Accretion-deletion is unique among cues to surface organization in its high reliability, occurring only at true object borders and never at internal texture borders.
source: In particular, among all cues to surface organization, accretion–deletion is unique in its (1) high reliability, occurring only at true object borders and never at internal texture borders, (2) robustness to object texture, and (3) computational power, supporting not only segmentation but also invariant tracking without requiring any learning or prior experience (Tsao and Tsao, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tsao and Tsao, 2022.

claim: Accretion-deletion is robust to object texture.
source: In particular, among all cues to surface organization, accretion–deletion is unique in its (1) high reliability, occurring only at true object borders and never at internal texture borders, (2) robustness to object texture, and (3) computational power, supporting not only segmentation but also invariant tracking without requiring any learning or prior experience (Tsao and Tsao, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tsao and Tsao, 2022.

claim: Accretion-deletion supports not only segmentation but also invariant tracking without requiring any learning or prior experience.
source: In particular, among all cues to surface organization, accretion–deletion is unique in its (1) high reliability, occurring only at true object borders and never at internal texture borders, (2) robustness to object texture, and (3) computational power, supporting not only segmentation but also invariant tracking without requiring any learning or prior experience (Tsao and Tsao, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tsao and Tsao, 2022.

claim: The finding that mice cannot detect figures defined purely by opponent motion is consistent with a previous study showing that rats could not learn to detect a bar defined by a grid of Gabor patches moving counterphase to ones in the background.
source: In particular, consistent with our finding that mice cannot detect naturalistic figures defined by opponent motion, Keyser et al. found that rats could not learn to detect a bar defined by a grid of Gabor patches moving counterphase to ones in the background (De Keyser et al., 2015) (note, however, their stimulus did not contain accretion–deletion, the cue we were especially interested in for reasons explained above).
evidence: This is supported by citation to De Keyser et al., 2015.

claim: Figure-ground signals exist in mouse visual cortex but are strongly dependent on texture.
source: Our finding that figure-ground signals exist in mouse visual cortex (Figures 3e, f, 4, and 5d, i), but are strongly dependent on texture (Figures 4 and 5a, b, e, i–k), is consistent with previous studies (Schnabel et al., 2018a; Kirchberger et al., 2020; Schnabel et al., 2018b; Keller et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is supported by neural data from multiple figures and citations to previous studies.

claim: Optogenetic perturbation studies have demonstrated that figure-ground signals in mouse visual cortex are behaviorally relevant for figure detection.
source: Optogenetic perturbation studies have further demonstrated that these signals are behaviorally relevant for figure detection (Kirchberger et al., 2020) and require feedback (Kirchberger et al., 2020; Keller et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kirchberger et al., 2020 and Keller et al., 2020a.

claim: Figure-ground signals in mouse visual cortex require feedback.
source: Optogenetic perturbation studies have further demonstrated that these signals are behaviorally relevant for figure detection (Kirchberger et al., 2020) and require feedback (Kirchberger et al., 2020; Keller et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kirchberger et al., 2020 and Keller et al., 2020a.

claim: Mouse visual cortex shows orientation-dependent surround modulation which can support texture-based figure-ground segmentation behavior.
source: Thus overall, it seems clear that mouse visual cortex shows orientation-dependent surround modulation (Self et al., 2014; Keller et al., 2020a) which can support texture-based figure-ground segmentation behavior.
evidence: This is supported by citations and is an inference from the data.

claim: Mice lack a general, texture-invariant mechanism for surface segmentation, unlike primates.
source: However, importantly, our results show that mice lack a general, texture-invariant mechanism for surface segmentation, unlike primates.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the behavioral and neural data.

claim: Cells selective for local motion have been reported in the retinas of both rabbits and mice.
source: The inability of mice to detect figures defined purely by opponent motion was rather surprising, as cells selective for local motion (distinct from global retinal image drift due to fixational eye movements) have been reported in the retinas of both rabbits and mice (Kim et al., 2015; Olveczky et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2015 and Olveczky et al., 2003.

claim: Retinal object-motion cells are unable to detect conditions where figure and ground move exactly in counterphase.
source: First, in our experiments, figure and ground moved exactly in counterphase, a condition that the retinal object-motion cells are unable to detect (Olveczky et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Olveczky et al., 2003.

claim: Mice were readily able to detect moving figures against stationary backgrounds.
source: We confirmed that mice were readily able to detect the same moving figures against stationary backgrounds (Figure 2—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2c.

claim: Deep networks fail to exploit global image features such as object boundaries and shape to perform classification, instead relying much more strongly on texture features.
source: Furthermore, recent work has shown that deep networks, unlike humans, fail to exploit global image features such as object boundaries and shape to perform classification, instead relying much more strongly on texture features (Brendel and Bethge, 2019; Geirhos et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brendel and Bethge, 2019 and Geirhos et al., 2018.

claim: A major difference between deep networks and the primate visual system lies in their segmentation capabilities.
source: Thus it is clear that a major difference between deep networks and the primate visual system lies in their segmentation capabilities.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited literature about deep networks and knowledge about primate vision.

claim: Mice may adopt a visual strategy more similar to deep networks than primates do.
source: Our finding of strong texture dependence in mouse segmentation behavior suggests that mice may adopt a visual strategy more similar to deep networks than primates do (Figure 7g; see also Vinken and Op de Beeck, 2020), though further detailed circuit dissection will be necessary to test this conjecture.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the similarity between mouse behavior and deep network performance.

claim: Accretion-deletion can enable texture-invariant segmentation and tracking without learning, thus it can provide a rich stream of training examples to self-supervise learning of other cues.
source: Rather, its chief importance is that it can enable texture-invariant segmentation and tracking without learning, thus it can provide a rich stream of training examples to self-supervise learning of other cues (Tsao and Tsao, 2022; Chen et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tsao and Tsao, 2022 and Chen et al., 2022.

claim: The discovery that non-primate brains are incapable of using accretion-deletion is highly ethologically significant because it means a key computational mechanism for self-supervised learning of a physical world model may be unique to primates.
source: In this respect, the discovery that non-primate brains are incapable of using accretion–deletion is highly ethologically significant, because it means a key computational mechanism for self-supervised learning of a physical world model may be unique to primates.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion about the broader significance of the findings.

claim: Adult mice 2-12 months old, both male and female, were used in this study.
source: The following animals were used in this study: adult mice 2–12 months old, both male and female; adult treeshrews 7–18 months old, both male and female; adult mouse lemurs 2–3.5 years, both male and female; and adult macaques 3 and 7 years old, male.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the animals used.

claim: Figure maps of neurons were highly stable across multiple days, with mean correlation between maps from matched cell pairs of 0.5579.
source: The mean correlation between maps from matched cell pairs across different days was very high (N = 950 cell pairs, Pearson r = 0.5579 matched vs. Pearson r = 0.2054 unmatched, KS test p = 1e−163, Figure 3g).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3g.

claim: The Cross stimulus completely fails as a behavioral marker for a nonlinear figure-ground segmentation process.
source: This underscores an important point: the Cross stimulus completely fails as a behavioral marker for a nonlinear figure-ground segmentation process (see also Vinken and Op de Beeck, 2021).
evidence: This is an inference from the modeling results and is supported by citation to Vinken and Op de Beeck, 2021.
